neighbours.label: semblance in literary narration: the word after 'seemed' / 'as if' / 'almost' that turns a description into an impression ('seemed as if', 'seemed to', 'almost fancied')
fire: The old house was so silent that it seemed as if nobody had lived there for years.
In the fog, the trees seemed to float above the road.
The night was long; it seemed as though morning would never come.
Her face was so pale that she seemed almost a ghost in the candlelight.
The ship lay so still that it seemed as if it hung in the air.
For a moment the whole crowd seemed to hold its breath.
He stood there so long that he almost fancied he had dreamed it.
The valley below seemed to glow under the last light of evening.
quiet: The old house was empty because the family had moved to the city years ago.
In the fog, the trees along the road were hard to see.
The night was long, and morning came at six o'clock.
Her face was pale in the candlelight after the long illness.
The ship lay at anchor in the harbor all afternoon.
For a moment the whole crowd was quiet before the speech.
He stood there for an hour and then went home.
The valley below was covered in wheat fields and orchards.
